situation: An async function uses Array.prototype.forEach with an async callback to perform work, then returns its accumulator immediately — forEach is fire-and-forget and ignores returned promises, so the function resolves before any item is processed, yielding empty/zero results.
deadEnds: Adding `await` in front of the forEach call — Array.prototype.forEach returns undefined, awaiting it does nothing
Switching to a plain `for...of` loop without awaiting inside — still misses concurrency or still races if the loop body is fire-and-forget
Trying to share a mutable accumulator across parallel async closures while assuming push order
Reaching for queueMicrotask/setImmediate/sleep hacks to 'wait for' the forEach callbacks to drain
unlock: Replace `forEach(async ...)` with `await Promise.all(arr.map(async ...))` (or a sequential `for...of` with `await` inside if ordering by side-effects matters), so the outer async function actually waits on every item's promise before returning.

situation: A read-style accessor on a recency-tracked data structure returns the value but fails to update the recency/access metadata, so subsequent eviction or ordering decisions treat the just-accessed item as if it were untouched.
deadEnds: Hunting for off-by-one errors in eviction threshold or capacity comparisons
Inspecting the doubly-linked-list pointer plumbing in addToFront / removeNode / evictLRU (which is correct)
Suspecting the duplicate-key update path in the write accessor (it already refreshes recency correctly)
Adding new state or counters instead of reusing the existing recency-update helper
unlock: On every successful read path, invoke the same recency-update helper that the write path uses before returning the value — both reads and writes must register as 'touches' for an access-ordered policy to be correct.

situation: A higher-order wrapper captures the caller's variadic arguments in a closure but invokes the wrapped function with no arguments (or stale ones), so values flow into the wrapper but are dropped before reaching the inner callable.
deadEnds: Suspecting the timer/scheduling primitive itself — the timer mechanics are fine; only the invocation site is wrong
Rewriting the closure-capture or storing args on an outer variable — unnecessary, the rest argument already lives in the lambda's closure
Touching the throttle/sibling function or generic type signature — the type already promises Parameters<T> are forwarded, the runtime call just doesn't honor it
unlock: At every call site of the wrapped function inside the higher-order wrapper, spread the captured rest-argument tuple (`fn(...args)`) so the forwarded arguments actually reach the inner callable.

situation: A recursive structural traversal handles only the 'plain container' branch of the type lattice — it correctly walks primitives and generic containers but lacks (a) special-case branches for non-plain reference types whose identity/semantics aren't captured by enumerating own keys, and (b) a memoization table keyed on already-visited references, so self-referential or shared-reference inputs either lose semantics or recurse forever.
deadEnds: Trying to fix the cycle-recursion failure alone without also handling the non-plain reference type
Using a Set<object> instead of a Map<object, clone>: it stops recursion but cannot return the previously-allocated clone
Allocating the clone, recursing into children, and then registering it in the seen-map — by the time a self-referential child is visited, the parent isn't registered yet
Reaching for JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) as a shortcut — drops Date semantics and throws on cycles
Special-casing the non-plain type via Object.assign/spread — meaningful state lives in internal slots, not enumerable own properties
unlock: Add an early-return branch for each non-plain reference type that reconstructs it via its own constructor/state-accessor before the generic object branch, AND thread a WeakMap<original, clone> through the recursion that is populated with the freshly-allocated container BEFORE descending into its children, so revisits return the in-progress clone instead of recursing.

situation: A subscribe/register helper wraps the caller's callback in a new function when registering it with an underlying API, but the matching unregister/teardown call passes the original (unwrapped) callback — so reference-equality-based removal silently no-ops and the listener leaks.
deadEnds: Assuming the bug is in the underlying remove method's filter predicate (it correctly uses ===); the predicate is fine, it's the argument that's wrong
Trying to make remove search by source-code or by-name equality instead of identity
Removing the wrapper entirely and passing the raw handler to register — works here but loses the abstraction the wrapper was added for
unlock: Capture the exact wrapped function in a local variable at registration time and pass that same reference to both the register and unregister calls, so identity-based removal matches.

situation: A two-pointer merge/zip routine over two sequences advances BOTH pointers when the heads are equal, instead of advancing only the side it just consumed — silently dropping duplicates that straddle the input partition.
deadEnds: Touching the split/midpoint math in the recursive divide step
Switching the comparator from <= to < (changes which side wins ties but still loses elements if both pointers advance per push)
Adding a 'dedupe equals' branch under the misconception that the spec wants unique values
unlock: In any merge/zip/interleave loop, each iteration must push exactly one element and advance exactly one source pointer; never piggyback a second pointer-advance on an equality check — let the next loop iteration handle the equal element from the other side naturally.

situation: Default-value fallback logic uses logical-OR (`||`) to substitute defaults, which incorrectly overrides legitimate falsy user inputs (0, '', false) with defaults — violating the contract that user-supplied values should win over defaults whenever they are actually present.
deadEnds: Adding extra explicit `=== undefined` guards per-field works but bloats the patch when `??` does the job in one character change
Reaching for `Object.assign({}, defaults, userConfig)` — tempting but wrong if the user object has explicit `undefined` values
Assuming the bug is in the test or in how Partial<T> is typed; the types are fine, the operator is wrong
Trying to special-case each falsy type instead of using the language-level nullish operator
unlock: Replace logical-OR (`||`) default-fallback with nullish-coalescing (`??`) so only `null` / `undefined` trigger the default, preserving falsy-but-intentional user values.

situation: A loop using an inclusive upper bound (hi = length - 1) is paired with a strict less-than continuation condition, causing the loop to skip the final candidate when the search window collapses to a single element.
deadEnds: Changing the midpoint formula or the branch update steps (mid+1 / mid-1) — these are already correct for an inclusive-bounds search
Switching to an exclusive upper bound (hi = length) without also changing the branch updates — the two conventions must stay consistent
Adding a post-loop check for arr[lo] === target — this masks the real issue
unlock: Match the loop's termination predicate to the bound convention: inclusive bounds (hi = n - 1) require `lo <= hi`; exclusive bounds (hi = n) require `lo < hi`. Pick one convention and keep predicate and updates internally consistent.

situation: An interval/window boundary is documented as inclusive, but the implementation uses a strict comparison operator that excludes the exact boundary value, causing off-by-one errors at edge timestamps.
deadEnds: Changing the cutoff arithmetic (e.g. using `now - windowMs + 1` or `now - windowMs - 1`) — this only shifts the off-by-one rather than fixing the inclusivity semantics
Modifying the length check from `>=` to `>` in the capacity guard — that changes throughput, not boundary behavior
Touching the timestamp push site — the bug is in the eviction predicate, not in insertion
unlock: When a spec says a boundary is inclusive, the predicate that retains/admits values at that boundary must use a non-strict comparison (`>=` or `<=`); audit every filter/guard that compares against `now - window` and ensure the operator matches the documented inclusivity.

situation: A recursive function over a recursive data structure has an over-eager base case that short-circuits at the leaf boundary and returns a value off-by-one from the rest of the recurrence (e.g. returning 0 for a leaf in a depth/size/count computation where the inductive case would have produced 1).
deadEnds: Adjusting the inductive return (e.g. changing `1 + max(...)` to `2 + max(...)`) to compensate — this breaks larger trees while only papering over the leaf case
Suspecting the null/empty base case when it is actually correct; the bug is in the *second* base case (the leaf shortcut), not the empty one
Rewriting iteratively or with BFS — unnecessary; the bug is a single wrong constant
unlock: Verify each base case independently by walking the smallest non-trivial input (a single leaf) by hand against the inductive case — if removing the special-case base would yield the correct answer via the inductive branch, the special case is either redundant or wrong; fix the constant or delete the branch.
